extracted.intended_audience: general Victorian readers; readers interested in political and social critique and reform
extracted.subtask_description: A literary essay critiquing 19th-century English institutions (Parliament, Law, Church, professions, and literature), arguing that society overvalues talk/appearance and undervalues silent performance, wisdom, and truth. Extracts normative claims about what qualities and selection criteria ought to matter in public and professional life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of industry (beaverism) and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial industry ('beaver career') yields national wealth but is only a half-result; it must be guided by wisdom to be truly good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor honest industrious contrivance, but beware when industry becomes the whole aim. The author praises 'beaver intellect' when it refuses vulpine shortcuts, yet insists wisdom must guide monetary success or it becomes baleful. Practical implication: evaluate professions and careers not only by their money-output but by whether wisdom directs that output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer performance (action) over mere talk
rubrics_metrics.description: The true function of intellect is understanding and discerning with a view to performing; talk, except as preparation for work, is worth almost nothing and can be destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly criticizes societies that reward eloquence over doing: 'Talk, except as the preparation for work, is worth almost nothing;--sometimes it is worth infinitely less than nothing.' Assess candidates and institutions by what they actually do and accomplish rather than by persuasive speech or rhetorical appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge merit by eloquence alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament, Church, and Law prove excellence by the tongue (ability to talk) rather than by silent work or real insight; this is a false proof of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection for office or prestige should be based on 'a good and just opinion worth speaking' and the ability to discern the law of a case, not merely on the ability to 'talk with due ability.' Evaluate aspirants by their insight and capacity for work rather than oratorical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for statesmen should prioritize true judgment over speaking skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman should be chosen for his capacity to 'discern with just insight' the law of the case and to follow it with valor, not because he can eloquently argue or 'make a speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice in Parliament may teach certain useful habits (patience, official courtesy) and how to navigate the institution, but it can mistrain men for real executive work. When evaluating political leaders, probe for genuine understanding and ability to act, not merely parliamentary polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicine should be a human, heroic healing vocation, not commercial beaverism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Physician's task is heroic and sacred; medicine should require wholly human intellect and should not be reduced to money-making, self-promotion, or quackery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of the 'half-articulate' drift where medicine yields a money-result alone or depends on 'ingenious talking' and publishing of oneself. Evaluate medical practice by its devotion to healing and integrity rather than by publicity or commercial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid professional preliminaries that demand incredibility or imposture
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain preliminaries (in Law and Church) require a candidate to declare belief in incredibilities or to 'constitute yourself an impostor' before entering; such requirements deter ingenuous talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional entry requirements should not force honest minds to accept falsehoods or insincere postures. When judging professional systems, treat mandatory dissimulation or credal imposture as a negative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature often becomes a refuge for vocables; value substantive truth in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature has become a crowded portal for 'vocables'—talk in writing—and a refuge for foiled ambitions and vanities; the duty laid upon the writer is too often merely to 'talk' well with pen or tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary work not merely by eloquence or talkative flourishes but by the substantive truth, insight, and work embodied in the writing. Distinguish mere vocables and sensational rhetoric from literature that conveys genuine wisdom or achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech must be subordinate to work; excessive talk is corrosive
rubrics_metrics.description: If intellect acquires the habit of talk, performance diminishes; talk is 'delightfully handy' compared with work and may lead to no work at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessment of individuals and institutions, penalize patterns where appearance and rhetorical activity substitute for substantive performance. Favor dispositions and systems that incentivize tangible outcomes and sustained work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness and breeding are necessary but insufficient for office
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners, patience, discretion, and politeness are indispensable preliminaries for office but are not a substitute for intrinsic qualities like understanding and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating candidates for office, treat cultivated manners as baseline qualifications; require demonstration of intrinsic qualities (dignity, insight, capacity for work) beyond mere civility and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom is primarily silent and proven by deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom cannot be fully expressed in words; it is 'intrinsically of silent nature' and is legible in presentiments, struggles, and ultimately in the man's completed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appraise wisdom by a person's conduct, work, and outcomes rather than by eloquent statements about their own capacities. Recognize that premature verbalization can obstruct the authentic demonstration of wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness is essential; voluntary divergence from fact (lying) is baseness
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary spoken divergence from fact is a lie and 'the essence of human treason and baseness'; such lies mislead practical dealing with facts and corrupt the speaker's capacity to think truly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make truthfulness a core criterion: distinguish between involuntary error (to be lamented) and voluntary falsehood (to be sanctioned). Evaluate speech and policy claims against facts; penalize deliberate misrepresentation severely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual loose speech degrades thought into falsity
rubrics_metrics.description: Loose tongues that articulate accepted commonplaces and cant lead to impalpable lying in thought: 'The lying thought... has long ceased to think truly in his mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the alignment of speech and thought. Persistent rhetorical insincerity tends to produce false internal judgments; when evaluating credibility, look for signs of habitual cant, glibness, or applause-seeking speech as predictors of unreliable judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions that train only talk can mistrain for essential functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament trains men to speak and endure foolish talk, but is a poor school for the intrinsic functions of a statesman; it can teach 'appearances' rather than real doing and even 'mistrain' officers for work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging institutions as training grounds, examine whether they cultivate genuine capacity to do work and to understand facts, or whether they primarily reward performative eloquence. Treat institutions that emphasize appearances as suspect for preparing leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition systems that require public proclamation disadvantage silent doers
rubrics_metrics.description: The worshipper of talk cannot recognize inarticulate veracity or an inarticulate Doer; excellence that does not proclaim itself can remain unrecognized because society demands articulation as proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation and recognition mechanisms that surface silent achievements (work products, outcomes) rather than relying solely on self-promotion or rhetorical proclamation. Be aware that market-demand for talk biases visibility toward talkers, not necessarily the best workers.
